source_title_hint: Don’t Stretch Your Tight Psoas. Do This Instead
primary_summary: This video explains that a tight psoas muscle is often a symptom of a forward center of gravity leading to anterior pelvic tilt and hyperlordosis, rather than a primary issue to be stretched. It demonstrates two exercises, a supine wall press with a foam roller and a standing wall press, to help shift the body's center of gravity back, rotate the pelvis posteriorly, and thus naturally lengthen the psoas.

classification.usefulness_reason: The video provides a biomechanical explanation for a common issue (tight psoas/anterior pelvic tilt) and offers specific, actionable corrective exercises with visual demonstrations and cues, making it valuable for diagnostic, explanation, and corrective exercise support.

key_visual_points: 3D anatomical model highlighting the psoas muscle and its connection to the lumbar spine and femur.
Demonstration of a person standing with anterior pelvic tilt and hyperlordosis, with a red line indicating a forward center of gravity.
Incorrect psoas stretch shown (lunge with arched back) marked with a red 'X'.
Skeleton model used to illustrate anterior pelvic tilt and the desired posterior pelvic rotation.
Demonstration of the supine wall press exercise with a foam roller between the knees.
Visual cues for foot contact points on the wall (heel, base of big toe, base of little toe, with emphasis on inner heel and big toe base).
Visual cue for feeling the PSIS (posterior superior iliac spines) on the ground.
Demonstration of the standing wall press exercise as a progression.
Visual cues for foot contact points and PSIS contact in the standing position.
Visual cue for reaching elbows away to create shoulder blade/spine separation.
exercises_mentioned: Supine Wall Press with Foam Roller
advice_mentioned: Do not just stretch a tight psoas; address the underlying body position.
Shift the body's center of gravity back.
Create a better ability to get the pelvis underneath you (posteriorly rotate).
warnings_or_limitations: During the supine wall press, do not press too hard into the wall or crunch the pelvis into the ground.

knowledge_units.title: Psoas Tightness as a Compensatory Mechanism
knowledge_units.summary: A tight or overactive psoas muscle is often a compensatory response to a forward-shifted center of gravity, leading to an anterior pelvic tilt and hyperlordosis, rather than being the primary problem itself. Simply stretching the psoas will not resolve the underlying postural issue.
mechanisms: The psoas is a hip flexor; when the body's center of gravity is pushed forward, the psoas shortens to help maintain an upright posture.
This shortening contributes to anterior pelvic tilt and increased lumbar lordosis.
Addressing the body's overall position and center of gravity is key to releasing psoas tension.

knowledge_units.title: Supine Wall Press with Foam Roller for Pelvic Repositioning
knowledge_units.summary: This exercise aims to shift the body's center of gravity posteriorly and encourage posterior pelvic rotation by establishing specific foot and pelvic contact points, thereby allowing the psoas to lengthen naturally. It emphasizes gentle effort and diaphragmatic breathing.
execution_steps: Lie on your back with your feet hip-width apart on a wall, ensuring your shins are parallel to the ground.
Place a foam roller between your mid-thighs.
Allow your chin to passively point at the ceiling, avoiding tension in the head or neck.
Push into the wall with your feet with a 1-2 out of 10 effort.
Focus on feeling three main points of contact on the wall: your heel, the base of your big toe, and the base of your little toe, with special emphasis on the inner heel and base of the big toe.
Gently feel your PSIS (posterior superior iliac spines) on the back of your pelvis move onto the ground.
For added benefit, bend your elbows and reach them low, feeling a gentle separation between your shoulder blades and spine.
Breathe in through your nose, allowing the air to fall into your back rib cage.
Exhale through your nose or mouth, gently letting the air fall out.
Maintain awareness of your head stacked over your rib cage, which is stacked over your pelvis, with the PSIS contacts on the ground.
cues: Push into the wall with 1-2/10 effort.
Feel your inner heel and base of big toe contact the wall.
Feel your PSIS gently move onto the ground.
Head stacked over rib cage, over pelvis.
breathing_cues: Inhale through your nose, let the air fall into your back rib cage.
Exhale through your nose or mouth, gently letting the air fall out of you.
errors_to_avoid: Pressing too hard into the wall.
Crunching or pushing the pelvis too much into the ground (over-tucking).
when_useful: To correct anterior pelvic tilt and hyperlordosis.
To shift a forward center of gravity posteriorly.
As an introduction to proper body stacking and alignment.

knowledge_units.title: Standing Wall Press for Upright Posture Progression
knowledge_units.summary: This exercise is a progression from the supine version, designed to transfer the learned pelvic alignment and center of gravity shift into an upright, standing posture. It focuses on maintaining proper foot and pelvic contact points against a wall while breathing.
execution_steps: Stand with your back against a wall.
Position your feet far enough away from the wall so that your knees are straight but not locked out.
Feel the same three foot contact points on the ground: your heel, the base of your big toe, and the base of your little toe.
Allow your eyes to stay straight ahead; your head does not necessarily need to be on the wall.
Actively feel your PSIS (posterior superior iliac spines) making contact with the wall (you may need to slightly bend your knees to achieve this).
Reach your elbows gently away from you, creating separation between your shoulder blades and spine.

Perform the same diaphragmatic breathing as in the supine exercise, bringing awareness to your head stacked over your rib cage, which is stacked over your pelvis, with your weight further back on your heels.
cues: Feel the same three foot contact points.
Feel your PSIS contacts on the wall.
Reach elbows gently away from you.
Head stacked over rib cage, over pelvis.
Weight further back on your heels.
breathing_cues: Inhale through your nose, let the air fall into your back rib cage.
Exhale through your nose or mouth, gently letting the air fall out of you.
when_useful: To progress pelvic alignment and center of gravity shift to an upright position.
To improve standing posture and reduce psoas tension in functional positions.

model_notes: The video effectively explains a common biomechanical misconception and provides practical, progressive exercises. The use of anatomical models and clear visual cues enhances its educational value. The emphasis on gentle effort and breathing aligns with principles of neuromuscular re-education.
